issues.title: Define issue-backed roadmap and release planning
issues.body:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**
APM's existing roadmap was retired in favor of a stale release milestone. Contributors and maintainers need a usable planning model that distinguishes visibility, priority, implementation approval, and release targeting without maintaining duplicate lists.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
Phase 3 of the governance/roadmap stack, explicitly approved by @danielmeppiel in the interactive planning session on 2026-09-11. Stack this PR on #2956, which depends on #2954.

Document ONE native GitHub Project with these views over actual issues:
- Intake: native auto-add of open microsoft/apm issues; visibility is not approval.
- Roadmap: selected issues grouped by one Horizon field (Now / Next / Later) and ordered by priority. Hide unselected intake items from the roadmap view.
- Ready to contribute: accepted, unclaimed help-wanted work, with contributors checking the human scope-approval record and review contact.
- Release: use the existing issue milestone, not a duplicate target-release field.

Document operating decisions:
- Now means active, reviewer-backed priorities; start with at most three strategic outcomes alongside necessary maintenance. Next is a ranked shortlist; Later is deferred consideration. Neither placement nor reactions authorize implementation or guarantee delivery.
- Anyone may propose outcomes through an issue. Area maintainers assess scope, risk, and maintenance cost; core maintainers shape the shortlist and the lead coordinates final ordering.
- Aim for a weekly asynchronous triage pass and monthly roadmap refresh, without turning these into response-time guarantees or a mandatory meeting bureaucracy.
- Milestones hold plausible release cohorts, not every accepted idea. Reconsider unfinished work explicitly at release time rather than automatically rolling everything forward.
- Larger outcomes use parent issues linking bounded implementation issues. Keep scope/approval on issues, horizon/order on the Project, and release targeting in milestones.

Acceptance criteria:
- GOVERNANCE.md owns the planning model and responsibilities; contributor entry points link to it without a second roadmap document or duplicated roster.
- The intended Project settings and final rollout steps are actionable using native GitHub capabilities, not a new planning platform.
- Existing approval rules, technical recipes, and maintainer roster remain unchanged.
- No Project creation/reopening, automation activation, live settings/labels/milestones, priority selection, or backlog population/cleanup occurs in this PR. Those actions remain in the final approved rollout.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
A pinned issue alone is insufficient as the maintainer's working planning surface. A custom planning system adds maintenance burden. Using milestones as the entire roadmap conflates product direction with delivery targets; manually copied roadmap lists will drift.

**Additional context**
Depends on #2955 / #2956. This is a small documentation-only layer unless a genuine implementation need is separately raised. Use a concise custom PR body, not the PR-description skill format. Phase 4 eligibility checks and final retrospective cleanup remain separate approval gates. Do not add fake live Project links or invent actual roadmap priorities.

issues.title: [BUG] Git-subpath dependency `content_hash` records CRLF bytes on Windows when the system gitconfig sets `core.autocrlf=true`; lockfile is not portable to Linux
issues.body:
**Describe the bug**

On a Windows host whose *system* gitconfig sets `core.autocrlf=true` (the Git for Windows installer default), `apm install` / `apm lock` materialize git-subpath dependencies (`owner/repo/<subdir>#<ref>`) with CRLF line endings. `compute_package_hash()` hashes raw bytes by design (see the docstring in `src/apm_cli/utils/content_hash.py`), so every package `content_hash` written to `apm.lock.yaml` is a CRLF-byte hash. The same commit materialized on Linux hashes differently, so:

- a lockfile generated on the Windows host fails `apm install --frozen` on a Linux runner with a content-hash mismatch, and
- a lockfile generated on Linux fails `apm install --frozen` on the Windows host.

This is the same failure class as #2187 and #2619, but the CRLF bytes here come from **git's own checkout of upstream content**, not from a synthetic file APM writes, so neither of those fixes covers it. `bare_cache.materialize_from_bare()` does run `git config core.autocrlf false` on the consumer clone before `git checkout` (src/apm_cli/deps/bare_cache.py, "CRLF determinism" block), but the materialized tree on this host still contains CRLF.

It is not a stale-cache artifact: with `APM_CACHE_DIR` pointed at a fresh empty directory the checkout is still CRLF.

**To Reproduce**

On Windows where `git config --system core.autocrlf` prints `true` and no user or repo config overrides it:

1. Create a manifest with one git-subpath dependency on any public repository whose text files are committed with LF, for example a skills directory:
   ```yaml
   dependencies:
     apm:
       - owner/repo/skills/<skill-name>#<tag>
   ```
2. Point apm at an empty cache and lock: `set APM_CACHE_DIR=%TEMP%\apm-cache-fresh` then `apm lock`.
3. Note the `content_hash` recorded for the dependency.
4. Lock the same manifest on Linux (or on the same Windows host with git's env-only override, see workaround). The `content_hash` differs.
5. `apm install --frozen` with the Windows lock on Linux reports a content-hash mismatch for the dependency.

I confirmed the cause by running apm's own `compute_package_hash()` over both materializations of the same commit: the CRLF tree reproduces the value in the Windows-generated lock, the LF tree reproduces the value the Linux runner computes. Checking the materialized checkout under `APM_CACHE_DIR` for `\r` bytes shows they are present on the Windows host and absent under the workaround.

**Expected behavior**

A git-subpath dependency at a pinned commit should hash identically on every OS regardless of the host's `core.autocrlf` setting. That is the invariant the `content_hash.py` docstring already states ("git-materialized content already does (identical bytes at a pinned commit on every OS)"). The per-clone `core.autocrlf=false` that `materialize_from_bare` sets should be sufficient. On this host it is not.

**Environment (please complete the following information):**

 - OS: Windows 11 (10.0.26300)
 - Python Version: 3.12.10
 - APM Version: 0.30.0 (a lock this host produced on an earlier 0.2x release shows the same class of mismatch, so it is not new in 0.30)
 - VSCode Version (if relevant): N/A
 - Git: 2.54.0.windows.1, system gitconfig `core.autocrlf=true`, no user or repo override
 - Linux side (for comparison): `apm-cli==0.30.0` on ubuntu-latest and in `python:3.12-slim`

**Logs**

`apm install --frozen` on Linux against the Windows-generated lock reports a content-hash mismatch per git-subpath package (expected = the CRLF hash in the lock, got = the LF hash). I can attach the exact output if useful.

**Additional context**

Workaround that fixes it completely: run apm with git's environment-only config override and a dedicated cache directory, so checkouts that were already materialized with CRLF are never reused:

```
GIT_CONFIG_COUNT=1
GIT_CONFIG_KEY_0=core.autocrlf
GIT_CONFIG_VALUE_0=false
APM_CACHE_DIR=<fresh dir>
```

With that in apm's environment the same `apm lock` records the LF hashes and the lockfile passes `apm install --frozen` on Linux. Setting `core.autocrlf=false` in `~/.gitconfig` also works. Both are host-side mitigations. The point of this issue is that a default Git for Windows install produces non-portable lockfiles out of the box, and nothing in apm's output says so.

UNVERIFIED hypothesis on the mechanism, for whoever picks this up: an env-level override fixes it while the per-repo `git config` in `materialize_from_bare` does not, which suggests some git invocation that writes working-tree bytes for these dependencies is not running against that consumer clone's config. Candidates: a different materialization path for subpath deps than `materialize_from_bare` (e.g. `GitCache._create_checkout`), or a copy step from the checkout into `apm_modules/` that goes through text mode. I have not traced it.

Related: #2187, #2619, #1952, and `scripts/crlf_invariance_probe.py`, which covers per-file hashing and APM-written synthetic files but not a real `core.autocrlf=true` git checkout of a subpath dependency through the package-hash path.

issues.title: [BUG] hook virtual package can't be installed with apm v0.29.1 and v0.30.0
issues.body:
## Describe the bug

Fresh installation with `apm install`  fails to install hook virtual packages.

## To Reproduce

I'll use podman to isolate the problem. 

```bash
podman container run -it --rm docker.io/library/ubuntu:noble-20260905
```

Inside a container:

```bash
apt update && apt install curl git -y
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
source $HOME/.local/bin/env
cd $(mktemp -d)
cat <<EOF > apm.yml
name: crabswarm
version: 1.0.0
description: APM project for crabswarm
author: ngicks
targets:
  - claude
  - codex
dependencies:
  apm:
    - git: github.com/ngicks/agents-package
      path: hooks/markdown-mermaid-lint
  mcp: []
scripts: {}
EOF
```

```bash
# uv tool install apm-cli@0.30.0

[>] Installing dependencies from apm.yml...
```

issues.title: [BUG] Lockfile writes replace symlinks instead of updating their targets
issues.body:
**Describe the bug**

When lock state changes, APM replaces a symlinked `apm.lock.yaml` with a regular file and leaves the link target unchanged.

This breaks setups where project or global lockfiles are symlinked to shared locations or dotfiles repositories.

**To Reproduce**

1. Create an `apm.yml` and a `shared.lock.yaml` that needs updating.
2. Run `ln -s shared.lock.yaml apm.lock.yaml`.
3. Run `apm lock`.

`apm.lock.yaml` is now a regular file; `shared.lock.yaml` is unchanged.

**Expected behavior**

APM preserves the symlink and writes the updated lockfile atomically to its target. If the target does not exist, APM creates it.

**Environment (please complete the following information):**

 - OS: Linux
 - Python Version: 3.12.14
 - APM Version: 0.29.0
 - VSCode Version (if relevant): N/A

**Logs**

The command exits successfully despite breaking the link:

```text
[+] Lockfile written to apm.lock.yaml
```

**Additional context**

`LockFile.write()` passes the symlink to `atomic_write_text()`, whose `os.replace()` call replaces the link itself. Resolving the final symlink before the atomic write preserves the link and updates its target.

issues.title: [FEATURE] Publish APM CLI releases with Packslip metadata
issues.body:
## Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.

APM already provides package-level reproducibility through `apm.yml` and `apm.lock.yaml`, but installing the APM CLI does not also give an agent version-matched guidance for using that CLI. Teams must provide their own instructions, and those instructions can drift from the installed APM version.

This creates practical problems for agents and developers. For example:

- An agent should know when to use `apm install` to reproduce the dependencies declared by a project.
- An agent investigating a dependency or content problem should know how to use `apm audit` and the lockfile.
- An agent preparing a package should know how to use `apm pack` and how the resulting package is distributed.
- An agent compiling configuration for a client should know when to use `apm compile -t copilot` or another supported target.
- An organization reviewing its agent dependencies should know how to export the lockfile as CycloneDX or SPDX with `apm lock export`.

These workflows need guidance that matches the installed CLI version. Consumers such as mise also need release metadata that identifies the correct APM artifact and the skills shipped with it. Packslip can connect those two needs without changing APM's package registry, dependency resolution, or package integrity checks.

## Describe the solution you'd like

Integrate the Packslip format into the APM CLI release process so each published APM CLI release can include a signed `packslip.sigstore.json` release manifest alongside its existing release assets.

The release workflow should:

- Generate a Packslip manifest from the final native release artifacts, after any archive rewriting, signing, or notarization.
- Record the `github.com/microsoft/apm` identity, version, artifact names and digests, supported platforms, formats, executable paths, and host requirements.
- Describe only resources shipped with the release, such as agent skills, if the release intentionally includes them.
- Sign and verify the manifest and artifacts before publication, then upload the manifest alongside the existing release assets.
- Document how Packslip-aware consumers can discover and verify the release. The format should remain consumer-neutral, with mise as one interoperability target.

The first version should publish accurate release metadata without changing existing APM installation paths or executing generated resource commands during publication. It succeeds when a Packslip-aware consumer can verify the official release identity and digest, select the correct platform artifact, and continue to use existing APM installation paths unchanged.

For example, a release could declare a versioned `apm` skill. The skill could give an agent guidance such as:

```text
Use `apm install` to install the dependencies declared in apm.yml.
Use `apm audit` to inspect package integrity and detect drift.
Use `apm pack` to bundle an agent package for distribution.
Use `apm compile -t copilot` to generate Copilot instructions from the project manifest.
Use `apm lock export --format cyclonedx` or `--format spdx` to create a software inventory.
```

The skill should be versioned with the CLI so that command names, options, and behavior remain aligned. After installing the Packslip-enabled CLI, a mise consumer could inspect and synchronize the declared skill:

```sh
mise use packslip:github.com/microsoft/apm
mise skills ls
mise skills sync --dir .agents/skills
```

The agent would then find the matching skill under `.agents/skills/apm/SKILL.md` and could apply it when helping with APM tasks.

Packslip can declare that skill in several ways. The paths below are illustrative and would need to match the published release layout:

```yaml
# Skill directory inside the selected CLI archive
resources: |
	skill/apm-release=archive:apm/share/skills/apm-release

# Skill distributed as a separate signed release asset
resources: |
	skill/apm-release=asset:dist/apm-release-skill.tar.gz

# Skill read from the source repository at the signed release commit
resources: |
	skill/apm-release=repo:.agents/skills/apm-release
```

Archive and asset sources are covered by signed digests; repository sources are pinned to the release commit. Generated `exec` skills should be a later, explicitly reviewed option because their output is not separately signed.

## Additional context

Packslip is a signed release manifest format for artifacts, platform selection, executable paths, host requirements, provenance links, and resources such as agent skills and SBOMs. Here it would describe the distribution of the APM CLI, while APM continues to manage agent packages and their dependencies.

Relevant references:

- [Mise skills CLI](https://mise.jdx.dev/cli/skills.html)
- [Mise Packslip resources](https://mise.jdx.dev/dev-tools/packslip-resources.html)
- [Packslip](https://packslip.dev/)
- [Packslip release specification](https://packslip.dev/release/v1/)
- [Packslip GitHub publishing guide](https://packslip.dev/docs/publishing/)

issues.title: [BUG] docs(install): local .apm/ deployment is documented as skipped at --global, but ~/.apm/ primitives do deploy
issues.body:
**Describe the bug**

The `apm install` reference documents local `.apm/` deployment as "Skipped at `--global` and with `--only mcp`" (`docs/src/content/docs/reference/cli/install.md`). The `--only mcp` half is correct; the `--global` half is not. At user scope the source root is `$HOME` (`get_source_root()` in `src/apm_cli/core/scope.py`), so `apm install -g` runs the phase against `~/.apm/` and deploys those primitives to user-scope targets.

The wording traces to #830, where `apm install -g` was walking all of `$HOME` looking for local primitives. That was resolved by scoping the walk to `~/.apm/`, not by skipping the phase, so the docs describe a skip that was never shipped. Readers who keep primitives in `~/.apm/` are told the supported path does not work and go hunting for a workaround.

**To Reproduce**

Verified on 0.31.0 (8fd10ac) against an isolated `HOME` containing:

```
~/.apm/apm.yml                             # targets: [claude]
~/.apm/instructions/demo.instructions.md
~/.apm/skills/demo-skill/SKILL.md
```

```
$ apm install -g
[>] Installing dependencies from apm.yml...
  [+] <project root> (local)
  |-- 1 rule(s) integrated -> .claude/rules/
  |-- 1 skill(s) integrated -> .claude/skills/
[*] Installed 1 APM dependency in 0.1s.

$ ls ~/.claude/rules/
demo.md
```

The same setup with `apm install -g --only mcp` deploys nothing, matching the documented `--only mcp` skip.

**Expected behavior**

The bullet lists `--only mcp` as the only skip condition and states the user-scope source root, so readers know `~/.apm/` primitives deploy to user-scope targets.

PR #2769 is open with the one-line correction.

**Environment**

- OS: macOS (Darwin 25.6.0)
- APM Version: 0.31.0 (8fd10ac)
- Documented claim still present at HEAD 707e8fa0

---

*Disclosure: this report was drafted with AI assistance; every command above was executed on the environment described.*

issues.title: [BUG] apm --version reports unrelated parent Git repository SHA
issues.body:
**Describe the bug**

`apm --version` can report an unrelated parent Git repository commit as though it were the APM build commit.

The packaged `apm_cli.version.get_build_sha()` has no injected `__BUILD_SHA__`. For a non-frozen installation it runs `git rev-parse --short HEAD` from its installed Python library directory. Git walks upward and may discover an unrelated ancestor repository.

**To Reproduce**

With APM 0.31.0 installed through Homebrew, run:

```console
$ apm --version
Agent Package Manager (APM) CLI version 0.31.0 (edb70f031e)
```

The displayed SHA belongs to the Homebrew repository rather than APM:

```console
$ git -C /opt/homebrew show -s --format='%H%n%s' edb70f031e
edb70f031e4170c780799633a1226ff73e1077f4
Merge pull request #24018 from Homebrew/sandbox-security-review
```

For comparison, the native APM v0.31.0 release archive reports:

```text
Agent Package Manager (APM) CLI version 0.31.0 (8fd10ac)
```

**Expected behavior**

Installed PyPI/Homebrew packages should either:

1. report a release SHA embedded during the package build, or
2. omit the SHA when no trustworthy APM source checkout can be identified.

Runtime Git fallback should only be used after proving that the resolved repository is the APM source checkout. It must not accept an arbitrary ancestor Git repository.

**Environment (please complete the following information):**

- OS: macOS
- Python Version: 3.14.7
- APM Version: 0.31.0 installed with the Homebrew core formula
- VSCode Version (if relevant): Not applicable

**Logs**

The relevant command output is included in the reproduction above.

#### [F] Sequential I/O with no data dependency -- src/apm_cli/registry/operations.py:292-310

- Current: O(n) sequential HTTP round-trips -- `batch_fetch_server_info` loops
  over `server_references` and calls `self.registry_client.find_server_by_reference(server_ref)`

issues.title: [perf-scan] 2026-09-24 -- performance opportunities found
issues.body:
## Performance Scan - 2026-09-24

Automated scan of src/apm_cli/ for algorithmic performance anti-patterns.
1 finding identified.

### Findings

#### [B] Linear scan inside a loop (set/dict opportunity) -- src/apm_cli/security/executables.py:312-337

- Current: O(P * G) per install -- `_map_grants` (line 312) does a full
  `for stored_key, entry in grant_map.items()` scan over the
  `allowExecutables` project/user grant maps. It is invoked once per
  candidate key per exec type from `resolve_exec_decision` (line 368),
  which is itself called once per package per declared exec type from
  `check_executable_approval` (src/apm_cli/install/exec_gate.py:57-90)
  during every `apm install`. With P installed packages each declaring
  grants, the effective cost across a full install is O(P^2) grant-map
  scans (each scan re-walks the same dict entries with a version-blind
  key-matching branch).
- Proposed: O(1) average per lookup with an O(G) one-time pre-compute.
  Build a `{name_or_key: {exec_type: bool}}` index once per
  `ExecTrustContext` (or lazily memoize it on first use), keyed on both
  the raw stored key and its version-stripped name, then have
  `_map_grants` do a direct dict lookup instead of iterating
  `grant_map.items()` on every call.
- Fix: Add a cached index (e.g. `ctx._grant_index` built once in
  `build_exec_trust_context`) mapping normalized package keys to their
  per-exec-type grants, and change `_map_grants` to look up that index
  by `package_key`/`name` instead of looping over `grant_map.items()`
  on every call.

### Scan coverage

- src/apm_cli/ (484 files scanned)
- Patterns checked: A (quadratic loops), B (linear scan in loop),
  C (unconditional expensive ops), D (redundant config parsing),
  E (heavy top-level imports), F (sequential independent I/O)

Most hot loops already use pre-built index dicts/sets (e.g.
uninstall/engine.py's exact_index/plugin_index, deployment_ledger.py,
registry/operations.py's ThreadPoolExecutor batches, context_optimizer.py's
glob caches), and CLI startup already lazy-imports heavyweight verb
modules (install, uninstall, prune, marketplace, pack, update, audit,
search, unpack) via cli.py's `_LazyCommand`. This finding is the one
clear remaining opportunity found in this pass.
